Well, one of the concerns that they had -- the Bosnian Serbs had, certainly, as we have seen reflected in many of the documents, was the concern that, in particular, Muslims would move into what they regarded as their areas. As we've seen, they have in the past discussed means to prevent that. In this portion, he seems to be assuring the delegates that that could not happen, because people wouldn't be able to move without a special permit. Presumably, the permit in question is issued by the entity that people want to move into. And if, presumably, Serbs wanted to move into the Serbian entity, they would be given such a permit, since, as we have also seen, that one of the things that they foresaw was that Serbs, for instance, would tend to migrate to the Serbian entity, something which they looked on favourably

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The previous sentence refers to total freedom of movement and moving from one constituent unit and taking up residence in another. Are those two sentences somehow in conflict, or is there a -- are they reconciled in the original B/C/S, or is there an explanation that assists us in understanding those two sentences together?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to look at the original here. Absolute freedom of movement, that is, settlement from one constituent unit to the other. From one constituent unit. Ah. In the original, it says -- here there is also absolute freedom of movement, that is, settlement from one constituent unit into another part of the same constituent unit. Therefore, any major resettlement without a special permit from one unit into another unit is not foreseen. So the freedom of movement relates to movement within a constituent unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I therefore understand that the translation is not correct in English, where it says: "This includes total freedom of movement, which means moving from one constituent unit and taking up residence in another."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It should read: "In another part of the same unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second highlighted section begins at the bottom of page 9, and it appears on page 10 of the B/C/S version, and that begins: "A constituent unit may consist of a number of separate parts."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That reflects the portion of the document which I read before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it continues on to the top of page 10 of the English translation, concluding the sentence: "Connect all the parts, the whole of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would leave the Muslims in five to six enclaves, Croats in two to three."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently - and again, we do not have all the maps that were under discussion here - the Bosnian Serb delegation presented a map that would have connected all of their territory but not that of the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the highlighted section found on page 14 of the English version and page 16 of the B/C/S version. In the English, that is the last paragraph of page 14, beginning with: "Another general impression."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, here Dr. Koljevic is speaking, supplementing Dr. Karadzic's remarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does he assess the significance of developments and their importance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He refers to the establishment of the SDS as being apparently, in his view, the most important development for the Bosnian Serbs in the recent past, then regionalisation, and then the current discussion of the establishment of a Serbian entity within BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I direct your attention next to the highlighted section on page 16 of the English version, and pages 18 to 19 of the B/C/S. In the English version, the highlighted section begins with the third full paragraph and the words: "On the other hand," and continues into the -- and the next paragraph that -- contains the next paragraph, and then a portion of the third paragraph, down to the section that: "Some of our people, whether consciously or not, make the job much more difficult."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that portion, does Dr. Karadzic address the ultimate goal and the pace at which it can be achieved?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what's being referred to here is the fact that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnian Serb negotiators, having gotten into this international forum, have run into some of the political reality in the outside world and have discovered that the international community, the European Community in particular - I think it's actually the European Union at this point in 1992 - would not countenance a partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, letting part of Bosnia and Herzegovina remain within Yugoslavia as the Serbs desired, whereas the rest would be an independent state or something. That was not on, but that was -- what was possible was the establishment of different ethnic units or cantons within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, this represents, from the Bosnian Serb point of view, a -- quite a retreat from the position that they had been adopting and that of course was reinforced by the plebiscite, that is, that they remain in Yugoslavia. So Dr. Karadzic and other leaders were at pains to emphasise to the deputies that the results of the negotiations so far were good and that if they resulted in an agreement along the lines that was foreseen, that that was just the first step toward their ultimate goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to page 19 of the English translation and page 22 of the B/C/S. You have highlighted two paragraphs, the first of which begins: "Our strategic goals are beginning to materialise." The last portion of the second paragraph highlighted is: "As the popular saying goes, if kicked out the door, go back through the window. You will still be in the same place."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see Dr. Karadzic addressing the issue of the significance of remaining within BH for the present. The important thing to achieve right now was to realise or confirm, establish, their internal borders within BH, that is, the limits within BH of the Serbian constituent unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with reference to the proverb quoted by Dr. Karadzic at the end, is that connected with his comment that what matters is that -- who cares about external borders. What matters is that the ones within BH become as wide as possible?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The idea here seems to be that - in the original, I would translate it more like as thick as possible - that the separation within Bosnia between the constituent -- prospective constituent ethnic units be as deep as possible, that is, that those borders be even more significant than the external borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 20 of the English translation and page 23 of the B/C/S translation. You've highlighted, as we see on the screen in the English translation, four paragraphs, beginning: "As I was a participant in the Lisbon talks, I would like to add a few remarks."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we now see Mr. Krajisnik adding his contribution to the extensive reports which have been given on the negotiations, especially by Dr. Karadzic and then by Dr. Koljevic. And here he lays out what he sees as the two options before the Serbian people at the present time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first of which is to fight by political means, to make the most, as a first phase, at the present time. And the second of which is to break off the talks and go for what we have done over the centuries, win our own territories by force?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 23 of the English translation and page 27 of the B/C/S, you've highlighted another portion.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at this point we're into discussion by the deputies at this point. Professor Milutin Najdanovic is speaking, I believe. He's identified as Ajdanovic in the record, so I presume that's Professor Najdanovic, who was a deputy in the Chamber of Citizens in the BH Assembly, and, of course, a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we could focus for a moment on that first highlight, which begins: "When the Croato-Serbian face-off begins," and ends: "Already now it should be signalled to the Serbian people that there may be territorial exchanges and relocations of the populations."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a rather obscure reference, probably in connection with the discussions going on with the Croats, or at least the idea that Croats are an important factor in this situation and that it may be advisable to work out a deal with them, which may entail some exchanges of population and territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move forward to page 44 of the English translation. That would be pages -- or the highlighted section would be shown on -- or captured within page 55 and 56 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 55 and 56, I guess the bottom of 55 and moving on into 56. Sorry. I know that I've been saying B/C/S translation. Forgive me for that. Of course, it's the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have Dr. Karadzic speaking again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the highlighted section, Dr. Karadzic is speaking about: "Keeping Bosnian Krajina from becoming an issue and the fear that if it does, Knin Krajina will be lost, that UN forces will be sent in, two zones will be created, with the UN in place, blacks and dark-skinned kids being born, with this and that, and they cannot allow that to be achieved because we are close to achieving our strategic objectives." Can you explain the context of those remarks, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as I indicated, Dr. Karadzic seems to be satisfied with the way the negotiations are heading. They haven't achieved everything they want, but they're certainly moving in the right direction, in his view. However, at this particular point in time, there is another recrudescence, if you will, of the movement within the Bosnian Krajina to proclaim their own republic up there, perhaps unite with the -- what is now the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Croatia. This will really upset the apple cart, in Dr. Karadzic's opinion. In fact, he -- I believe in the course of this session, had to leave the session to take a telephone call from Ambassador Cutilheiro, who had received a letter from Mr. Izetbegovic complaining about this sort of thing, and so he's very concerned that the people -- the leaders in Bosnian Krajina will upset the apple cart, so to speak, and something which could lead to the consequences he's setting out here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one clarification. The text reads: "With UN in place, with blacks and dark-skinned kids being born, with this and that."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- how should I understand this part of the speech? Or at least, how do you think I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe the reference here is to a phenomenon which was seen in Germany after World War I, when portions of that country, the Rheinland in particular, were occupied by foreign troops, in particular, French, British, and American troops, among whom there were black troops, and a number of children were born out of unions between those black soldiers and German women, who were not very popular in Germany. They were referred to as the Rheinland bastards. So I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That explains your view on it. Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've next highlighted another portion of the same -- or of the remarks by Dr. Karadzic that appear on the next page. That's page 45 of the English translation and pages 57 through 58 of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Karadzic continuing. Here he's continuing to address the discipline problems as he sees them in Bosnian Krajina and reminding the deputies that once the party has adopted a policy, it has to be adhered to. We saw that at the beginning of this presentation within the party statutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the record, the highlighted section begins: "However, once the party has adopted a policy, anything else is treason," and ends with the sentence: "I will signal to the people: People, this man is a traitor."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to page 46 of the English translation and page 58 of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what page in the original?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 58. We find highlighted in the English translation a passage which begins: "I believe this is what we need to decide. This Assembly is a supreme organ. And if it or any other assembly makes a wrong move, this Assembly has the right to cancel those decisions."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Karadzic continuing on the theme of the problems in Bosnian Krajina and pointing out that the Bosnian Serb Assembly should impose a line on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to page 57 of the English translation and pages 73 through 74 of the B/C/S original. I have a note that the speaker is Goran Zekic, but you need to check and confirm that for us, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 73 and 74?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what my notes indicate. The highlighted section begins: "They would accept it only on condition that we make further concessions, but we have no reason to do so. We have no reason to preserve any kind of a Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes. I now have the place, and that is in fact Goran Zekic, who we have met before, a deputy and member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Zekic's remarks continue on to the next page of the English translation, concluding with the sentence: "And that is our task, because if our state, Yugoslavia, was destroyed, we shall destroy this Bosnia with all the means available." And the transcript indicates applause.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see here, there's quite a bit of support among the deputies for, not surprisingly, the line that had been taken all along, remaining in Yugoslavia, and they're having trouble dealing with a situation in which, as Dr. Karadzic is telling them, there may be an agreement which will not include that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to page 62 of the English translation, pages 74 through 75 of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have Mr. Kupresanin speaking, who we've met many times before, a -- one of the deputies and Main Board member and president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Treanor. But if I can interrupt you. I moved forward to the next item you had highlighted, overlooking Mr. Kupresanin, so I --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you said 74, 75. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could address the remarks by Mr. Kupresanin if you wish or we can move on to the next highlighted obviously. It depends on you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page are we on in the original, then, at this point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're moving forward to a passage which is contained on both pages 74 through 75 of the original. It begins on page 74 and continues to 75. On the English, it is on page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you not creating confusion? What I see in the English version on page 62 is a speech which, according to page 61, is delivered by Mr. Krajisnik, where on pages 74 and 75 of the original B/C/S, from what I can decipher, it's a speech delivered by Mr. Kupresanin. So I wonder whether you are not actually referring, if you are talking about page 62 of the English translation, to the bottom of page 77, continuing on page 78 and following. I'm afraid that you're mixing up parts of the English translation with the originals in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that certainly appears to be the case, Your Honour, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you want to talk about page 62 in English, you perhaps could guide the witness to page 77 and following of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can find it, based upon the assistance offered by the Court, again, the highlighted section in English, to which I was referring, begins with: "This attempt to impose Banja Luka, you can put it forward and embellish it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. I see that the highlighted text in the original, the B/C/S original, appears just in the middle of page 78.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And this is Mr. Mirko Mijatovic speaking, who was elected originally as a member of the Council of Municipalities. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry. Again I have to give an opportunity to the interpreters to translate. What I see is the highlighted portion in the middle of page 62 in English, seems to be something that has been said by Mr. Krajisnik and which appears on page 78 of the original, to be more precise in the middle of the page. I take it the paragraph starting with [B/C/S spoken] Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour. A lot of confusion in identifying these passages, unnecessarily, I'm sure. Yes, this is Mr. Krajisnik who speaks after short remarks by Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Treanor, if I could ask you then, now that I believe we have identified fully the passage, to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Krajisnik's commentary on the developments in Bosnian Krajina and in Banja Luka. I could mention in this regard that a meeting of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina had been scheduled for the end of the month of February, and this was the forum in which it was feared that certain decisions might be taken that would upset the negotiations that the main Bosnian Serb leaders were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe Mr. Krajisnik's remarks continue on to page 63 of the English and page 79 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've highlighted two portions of those, the first of which begins: "Gentlemen, we want to remain in a single state," and continues to the sentence -- or to the two sentences: "If we don't want to do this by certain methods, let us put a stop to it. You know what our profession has always been, to wage war."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This, I think, is along the lines of Mr. Krajisnik's earlier comment, that there are two ways toward the final goal; one, negotiations, which they're engaged in, and if you don't like the way those are going, the only alternative is to break them off and go to war to achieve them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second highlighted section on that page is found at the end of his remarks and begins with the sentence: "We have the opportunity to preserve the Serbian people in a single state."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here we see Mr. Krajisnik expressing his belief that this -- the negotiations in fact do present an opportunity to do that, as he had put it earlier, they're just the first step in that direction, and he's assuring the delegates that this is the way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next document that we'll move to is contained in binder 9, at tab 94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, tab 94 contains the record of the 28 February 1992 Deputies' Club. Before you direct your attention to selected portions of that meeting, are there any preliminary comments you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of points. One is that there had been a further negotiating session, under international auspices, in Sarajevo, on the 27th of February. At those negotiations, the international negotiators consulted not only the representatives of the three principal parties in BH, that is, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, but there was also a delegation composed of so-called independent deputies from the BH Assembly. That delegation was headed by Dragan Kalinic, who was, in fact, technically an independent member of the BH Assembly, but he was also a member of the Assembly of the Serbian People and has spoken at some of the sessions we've been considering. In connection with that particular session of the negotiations, the important point is that by this time, Mr. Izetbegovic had drawn back on his previous acceptance of the Lisbon document of the 23rd of February. As the Court will remember, that was -- that document was based on the idea of cantonisation. Three different constituent units, that type of set-up for BH, and this was an idea that the SDA had never favoured. And for whatever reason, Mr. Izetbegovic was drawing back a bit on this, and so the negotiations had to pick up at a different point from where they left off in Lisbon. The session we're about to consider is a session of the Deputies' Club per se, and it immediately precedes another session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which had been scheduled for that day. That session was -- the business of that session was basically to formally adopt the constitution which had been drafted and some of the associated legislation, setting up the organs of the Bosnian Serb Republic. The business of that session was therefore fairly ceremonious. During the preceding session of the Deputies' Club, which we're about to consider, this is where the deputies got Dr. Karadzic's report on the negotiations and where they had some more discussion about the draft constitution. This is a much longer session than the following assembly session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think we can make some headway on the document, although we have five minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you'd prefer to have the break now, that would be no problem, perhaps before we start this document, rather than stop halfway. We would then adjourn until 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that we have received a -- what it says now, a translation, although it's fuller than the previous translation, which was indicated as a full translation. Mr. Tieger, could you please guide us again to where to start, to what binder and to what number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm pleased to do that, Your Honour. It appears in tab 86 of binder 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you were about to address the 28 February 1992 Deputies' Club. If we could move, then, to the first highlighted section, which appears on page 4 of the English translation and page 5 of the B/C/S original. That is a highlighted section at the bottom of page 4 which begins: "Bosnia and Herzegovina will remain in Yugoslavia until we say it has left Yugoslavia," and concludes: "If they want independence, then we want independence too."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Krajisnik [sic] giving the deputies a report on the state of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I believe you just said Dr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference in that passage to the comment, as Mr. Krajisnik says: "Muslims who used to be a religious sect and have recently been given the status of a people," can you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we saw a remark similar to this, perhaps yesterday. I'm not sure who made it. This is a reference to the fact that the Muslims within Yugoslavia were only recognised as a people, that is, on an equal level with, say, the Serbs and the Croats and the Slovenes within Yugoslavia, beginning in the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move, then, to page 6 of the English translation and page 7 of the B/C/S original. You have highlighted the fourth paragraph of that page, as appears in the English, beginning: "Finally, the argument we used with the foreigners is very strong."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Karadzic continuing his report, and again here we can see a reference to the situation in India and Pakistan, as well as in Cyprus and Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that reference contains allusions to separation in a bloody way and a huge resettlement of the population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to page 9 of the English translation and page 11 of the B/C/S. There are two highlighted portions there. If you could identify the speaker and indicate the significance, pertinence of those highlights?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have Mr. Krajisnik speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first highlight is the first full paragraph of page 9 in the English, which begins: "They want it not because BH should be a state, but they want not to create an Islamic state in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's voicing his perception that one reason why the international community in particular wants BH to stay together is so that it will not become an Islamic state, and therefore they want to keep the Serbs and the Croats within the same state as the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second highlighted section is found in the middle of the page, and is two paragraphs, the first of which begins: "I have to disappoint you, deputies from the BH Assembly, the BH that once was probably is no more." And the second paragraph ends with a comment: "Then they looked at possibilities for Herzegovina, where it is. There's nothing down there, some green by the Neretva River, the part that is our strategic commitment."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here he's discussing the -- some of the nitty-gritty of the discussions with maps and that sort of thing. The inference -- reference to the Neretva at the bottom is interesting, in view of especially some later documents, which we'll see, a reflection perhaps of the Serbian desire, later expressed explicitly, to make the Neretva River one of the boundaries of their entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we move to the next page, page 10 of the English, page 13 of the B/C/S, is that a continuation of Mr. Krajisnik's remarks?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The highlighted section is the first full paragraph of that page, beginning: "In the end, we told them that the meeting would be organised between 5 and 10 March," and referring to the adoption of the constitution of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interesting passage, in which Mr. Krajisnik relates the reaction of the international negotiators to the news that the Bosnian Serbs were about to adopt their own constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning next to page 19 of the English translation and page 27 of the B/C/S. In the middle of the page we can see highlighted on screen a sentence: "I propose that our leaders, I mean Messrs. Karadzic and Krajisnik, must go to Banja Luka, but everything must be very well prepared for."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a remark by Mr. Zlatko Kelecevic, who was a deputy originally elected to the Chamber of Municipalities in 1990 from the Bosnian Krajina region, and he is again referring to the situation in Bosnian Krajina and the fact that the meeting for the Assembly there is now scheduled for the next day, the 29th of February. And it's his desire, and that of some of the other deputies, that the -- at the very least, the top SDS leaders go there to make sure that things go well. There were even calls for all the deputies to go up there. There was some fear that in fact non-SDS elements were sort of invading the meetings of the Assembly up there and pushing things along, according to their agenda rather than the SDS agenda, so that's one of the concerns they had about what might happen at that meeting and the desire for the presence of a strong SDS representation at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 28 of the English translation. That is page 41 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have Mr. Marinko Kontic speaking, one of the deputies originally elected to the Chamber of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The highlighted portion begins: "However, I personally have to criticise my great friend Vojo," and then continues: "The president of the Assembly," that's Mr. Krajisnik, "has shown that he has to control the Assembly. Mr. Kupresanin, likewise, has to control the situation in the Krajina Assembly."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reference here is to Mr. Kupresanin, who was the president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and Mr. Kontic is expressing some dissatisfaction with the way things -- he has handled things up there. He seems to think as president of the Assembly he should have been able to keep matters under control the way Mr. Krajisnik keeps things under control in the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to page 34 of the English translation, page 49 of the B/C/S. Two highlighted portions appear here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dr. Karadzic again referring to the situation within the party and the need for party discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The highlight to which you've just referred and which is currently shown on screen begins: "The Serbian Democratic Party is in power there." And continues with the next paragraph which begins: "First we should make it clear who in the Serbian Party does not comply with party discipline."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next highlighted portion is found below that, in the fourth and third paragraphs respectively from the bottom, beginning with: "It's not that easy to make a state. If it were possible to do it that way, ask Krajisnik how many times we have discussed this. If it were possible to do it that way." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here Dr. Karadzic is continuing to address the situation in Bosnian Krajina and saying that things aren't quite as simple as some of the people in Krajina might think they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I take it that we now moved to page 50 of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to page 36 of the English translation and page 52 of the B/C/S. There are two highlights in the upper portion of the page, and they represent three paragraphs, the first of which begins: "Imagine the stupidity of it: The conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is basically a conflict among peoples," the second of which begins: "Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear on that," and the third, which begins": "Yet they set up the Bosnian Krajina there and in two years' time you will have problems again, to separate each and every village there, because they will overwhelm you with their birth rate and their tricks. We cannot allow that to happen."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see the reference to the situation in India and Pakistan again, and Dr. Karadzic refers to the idea of setting up some sort of Krajina state, saying that if they do that, they've still got the Muslims in there and that won't work in the long run.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next page, page 37, you've also highlighted a section. Those are three paragraphs in the bottom half of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I may not have given the B/C/S. That is page 54.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is still Dr. Karadzic speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first paragraph begins: "Please, until two or three months ago, we were hoping to be able to play the Yugoslav card," and the second begins: "We are preparing the constitutional framework to be able to have immediately, and on the basis of the negotiations in Lisbon, to have a National Guard, to have our own police," and the third of which begins: "We have to play the interim moves."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a reflection of the fact that Dr. Karadzic perceives that the original idea of simply remaining within Yugoslavia was not immediately attainable for the Bosnian Serbs, and therefore, they are taking some interim steps, but in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference at the end is again to the idea of setting up a Bosnian Krajina state which -- within Yugoslavia, that this is one of the areas in which -- among the leaders of which this idea of -- that we're not going to -- where dissatisfaction was created by the prospect that they would not in fact immediately remain within Yugoslavia or continue to remain in Yugoslavia uninterruptedly, but may have to wait a while, and some people saw a solution for this, the proclamation of a state in Krajina, and Dr. Karadzic is I think saying here: Well, if they do that, then this will just get Serbia in trouble, and the main goal of some of the international factors is to destroy Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next highlighted section appears on the following page, page 38 of the English, page 55 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the end of Dr. Karadzic's remarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first highlighted section begins at the top of the page, which says: "What do we want? We want to realise our sovereign right, our state-forming right here where we are, and whether we will one day create ties with Serbia, when, and to what extent, that's not their business."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a reflection of the step-by-step approach that he is now advocating. As I indicated earlier today, he was very anxious to get the agreement on the partition, the transformation, the cantonisation, whatever you want to call it, of BH in place, in a manner satisfactory to them, before BH was recognised as an independent state, so that after that happened, they would be able to follow their own line as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition, on that page, there are two paragraphs highlighted, the first of which begins: "We are halfway there, no, not halfway. We've achieved 90 per cent of the things," and the second of which begins: "There will be other criteria, but the ethnic criterion will be the basic criterion."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here again he's emphasising to the deputies the great progress that has been made toward their ultimate goal. The reference is to the fact that one of the things that Mr. Izetbegovic objected to in the previous document, the document of the 23rd, was that ethnic -- the ethnic criterion seemed to be the only criterion for the establishment of the constituent units. He wanted other criteria to be used as well, as mentioned here, but Dr. Karadzic is assuring the deputies that the ethnic criterion will remain the principal criterion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question in this respect. The English text says ethnic criterion. The original text seems to say national or -- criteria of the nations. Is that correct? And are they interchangeable for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are different words in B/C/S. There are any number of words. The -- looking at this and seeing ethnic criterion, I would have expected to see the B/C/S word that is akin to that word, "etnicki." However, in the original, as Your Honour has pointed out, we see "nacionalni." Another option would be -- well, there might be other options, but I think as a matter of practicality, it's the same thing. The reference is to the national communities that we've been referring to, the three main national communities in BH: The Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say for practical reasons in this context they are interchangeable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn now to page 43 of the English translation, which is page 63 through 64 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, here we have Mr. Krajisnik speaking again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have highlighted the -- on that page, the paragraph which appears immediately above the last sentence appearing on the page, which begins: "The recommendations are: We don't need a confederal Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is unreasonable. We need only a single monolithic Serbian state, with a single centre."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here we see the reference to stages in the realisation of their goals. At the beginning of the passage, we see reference to the regionalisation idea within the Serbian entity, as has been mentioned. The Serbian Republic, which has been proclaimed, is composed of the territories of the previously existing Serbian autonomous districts. Some people seem to think that maybe that's a little bit too much, that the Serbian entity itself is, so to speak, a region of Bosnia and will be given its own sovereignty, so what is the sense of having regions within that entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final highlighted selection of this meeting is found on page 44 of the English translation and page 65 of the B/C/S. Is this still Mr. Krajisnik speaking?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Krajisnik getting toward the end of his remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the record, the highlighted portion would be the first -- would be the last three paragraphs, I believe, the first of which begins: "As for what Mr. Koljevic has said, I apologise. I never make long speeches," and then goes on into a list: "We are telling you straight what it is that they want. They want the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They want the currency. They want a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. They want an Islamic state." And the last paragraph contains -- begins with a reference: "But that will not succeed. We are a force to be reckoned with. We will not agree to that." And then mentions the line: "We will come here and explain. We will say: Dear gentlemen, get your woolen socks ready. We will go and defend ourselves." And then has two concluding sentences -- three concluding sentences, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see an exhortation to the deputies to have confidence in their negotiators in their delegation. He enumerates the types of demands that they are being faced with and assures them that they will never give in to these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say the types of -- excuse me. You mentioned the types of demands they are faced with. Are these demands actually made at the negotiations or a projection of the perceived threat faced by a unitary or --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this is his perception of what the real desires of the SDA are. And he, at the end, indicates that if they can't come to an agreement, they will inform the Assembly of that and tell them that it is necessary to get ready for war in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next selected document is found on tab 95, and that is a record of the 9th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, held on 28 January 1992, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard you say 28th of January, Mr. Tieger, and that's what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document, however, indicates that it would have been the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Quite right, and I simply made an error in speaking on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if I recall correctly, I think you indicated earlier that this was in large measure a ceremonial or ceremonious occasion. If you could just give us a quick backdrop and we'll move into the document quickly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is a session that followed the meeting of the Deputies' Club. This session began at five minutes after 4.00 in the afternoon and concluded -- that is, at 1605, and concluded at 1955 hours, in the course of which the Assembly formally adopted a constitution for the Serbian Republic, a constitutional law to implement that constitution, and some associated legislation to give form to the new state organs, including a law on the government, a law on defence, and a law on internal affairs. The larger package of legislation that was being considered over the previous month was not entirely ready at this point, so they did not adopt all the legislation they had projected, but did adopt these particular basic documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I note there are only a few highlighted portions of this particular section. If we could move to the first, which is found on page 6 of the English translation. Mr. Treanor, I'll have to rely upon you, once you find that, to indicate for the record where the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I don't have anything marked in this particular session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the portion marked is, as we can see from the screen, a brief portion of the comments by Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Maksimovic is, of course, the chairman -- president of the Deputies' Club. He would have been presiding at the previous meeting. At this meeting, Mr. Krajisnik is presiding, and he -- Mr. Maksimovic is here expressing his emotions at the adoption of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, because that's not as precise a reference as a page number, I want to ensure that Mr. Krajisnik has found that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, you guided us to page 6 of the English version, indicating -- and that's what I see on the screen as well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's page 8 of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 8. Yes, but I see -- let me just check. We are in tab 95, and you're guiding us to page 6 of the English version, which seems ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On our page 6, we do not see the name of Professor Vojislav Maksimovic underlined appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might indicate that it appears to be on actually page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a -- well, on page 12, Mr. Maksimovic is not underlined as well. But on page 11, as a matter of fact, it is. And then the highlight would then be on our page 12, and we see again that we have different documents, Mr. Tieger, because the part starting with: "The joy I feel cannot be diminished," appears in our hard copy on page 12, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. third line from the top. So since we've found now the English version, perhaps we could try to ... It seems to me that -- yes, it's page 8 of the B/C/S original. Are we all on track? Let's then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise for that discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I believe you've already addressed that comment, but I can only say for the record that -- which would be a bit confusing in this circumstance, and I will ensure that that discrepancy is reconciled immediately, Your Honour, that the portion which is highlighted is the fourth paragraph of Mr. Maksimovic's comments on whatever page number. It begins -- and I'm hesitant to refer to anything other than that the page number the Court has in front of it, but we see a different page number on the screen. We will reconcile that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have different ERN numbers, as a matter of fact, on the top of our pages. So these are two different documents, the one being more densely printed than the one we have. But we've found our -- the highlighted spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I indicated a moment ago when I began to ask Mr. Treanor the question, there are only very few highlights in this session. I don't think it will affect our progress if we move immediately to the document found at tab 96. I can ask Mr. Treanor for -- obviously, for his view on that, but he's explained the nature of the session, in particular, the decisions that were reached, and I believe we can move forward to some of the decisions that were made and the documents they reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it up to you. The only important thing for the Chamber at this moment is that the document you're referring to has the same content as the one we have in front of us, and I would very much appreciate if we could receive a copy with the same ERN numbers or one of your copies. But if it's the same text, then of course I would not mind if you proceed at this moment, but it should be verified and it should be confirmed to the Chamber that the text is the same and then our text should be replaced by the ones with the numbers on the top of the pages as we see them on the screen. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will make sure that that replacement takes place today, Your Honour. I think we can move on to tab 96, which is the decision on proclaiming the constitution. I'm sorry. Before we do that, I think it would be useful, however, to finish, for the record, the citation to that portion of the comments by Mr. Maksimovic that we've already referred to, which continues: "By referring to the irreconcilable opponents in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Europe, which we have long seen and continue to see today manifested daily in a very extreme form." And because the next selection appears only two sentences after that, I don't think the record would be unduly confused by noting that it is two sentences -- or it consists of two sentences which read: "This is the realisation of yet another significant step on the road towards realisation of our final political and national goals, and that is the creation of a state community of all Serbian lands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for confirmation. The text would exactly be the same. I now already come to the conclusion that the text is not the same, because it seems that although the original text may be the same, the translations are not the same. May I ask your attention for the last sentence of the first highlighted portion, where it reads: "Which we have long seen and continue to see today manifested daily in a very extreme form," whereas in the hard copy we have got in front of us, it reads: "It's still present in a very extreme form and is being manifested every day." I'm not saying that the content is not approximately the same, but certainly the text is not the same. So perhaps we should skip this part as well, having -- working from two different documents, and move on to 96, and you'll have an opportunity, once these texts are replaced, to ask questions on the basis of a text the same for Mr. Treanor as for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, turning to tab 96, we see the decision on proclaiming the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is, as published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, published on the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2 of that document, you've indicated some highlights, to which you wish to draw our attention. Those consist of Articles 1, 2, 3, and 5.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are some general articles that I'd like to call the Court's attention to before we consider the individual organs of power that were set up by the constitution and the related legislation. The Court will note that in Article 1, the republic is defined as the state of the Serbian people and of the citizens living in it. The word "all" is not in the original. This is in contrast to the similar provision in the BH constitution that I mentioned at the beginning of my presentation, which mentioned three peoples. So this state, as the article defines it, is a state of only one people. The Bosnian Serb leaders, of course, had premised much of their position and action on the fact that within BH, they were one of the constituent peoples, and therefore had certain rights as a people. Therefore, I think it's safe to say that under this article, only one people is being given rights as a people. Article 2 defines the territories -- the territory of the republic in terms which we've seen already, rather imprecise. It refers to the autonomous regions and municipalities. It then goes on to enumerate, including regions in which genocide was committed against the Serbian people in World War II. So there is no precise definition of boundaries. And then Article 3, the statement that the republic is part of the Federal State of Yugoslavia. There is no reference here, for instance, to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And now Article 5 encompasses some of the basic guarantees, basic principles of the constitutional order, including the guarantee and protection of human freedoms and rights and the protection of rights of ethnic groups and other minorities. And there is a reference just above that to regional autonomy and local self-government. This constitution does, in fact, make provision for the existence of regions within the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 28 February 1992 constitutional law for implementing the constitution is the next document you've selected. That's found at tab 99.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're getting into a consideration now of the main organs of power which were established by the constitution. Those organs, the ones that we will be considering in particular, are the National Assembly, the government, and the office of the presidents of the Republic. The powers and other related issues -- other issues related to those organs are specified in the constitution; however, at the same time, a constitutional law was adopted which provided for provisional measures that would be applied until the provisions of the constitution per se could be fully implemented. That constitution, for instance, would have required -- to implement that constitution would have required the holding of elections and that type of thing. So we have transitional provisions in the constitutional law, and Article 3 relates to the National Assembly. It provides for a provisional National Assembly, if you will, until it's possible to hold elections. The definition of a National Assembly is basically the same as the definition of the Assembly of the Serbian People, that is, the deputies of Serbian nationality who were elected in 1990 to the Assembly of BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could return to tab 96, the decision on proclaiming the constitution, and begin discussing the various organs that were set up and the competencies, authorities, and roles assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. What we have here now, this is the constitution per se. The decision on proclaiming the constitution is immediately followed by the text of the constitution which was being proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, the portion of the document that you now see on screen is found at page 11, and I'll attempt to guide the Court through those pages successively. And page 22 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, as we move through the organs, although the Court may guide you, seek particular information about particular sections, I think I would ask you to move through those as quickly as possible, identifying the portions of the constitution where they appear, the general terms of those articles and provisions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning first to Article 69, again found at page 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the article that sets out the basic organs, essential organs of power within the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 70, the next highlighted section, is found at page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a basic article enumerating the responsibilities of the National Assembly within the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Article 74, found on that same page.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This makes some mention of the responsibility, powers and responsibility of the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to Article 87, I believe. That's found at page 14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a simple article dealing with a facet of the office of the presidents of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it indicate further who would assume his term of office should he be unable to fulfil his duties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see provision for the president of the National Assembly to act for the president in certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the next article you've highlighted is Article 90, found at page 15.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see the basic article enumerating the responsibilities of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 94 on that same page.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article specifying that the government is responsible to the Assembly and how no-confidence can be voted in the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few pages are missing on one of the copies. For the time being, we'll share our copy, and if you could please provide page 15 and 16 again for Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, anything further about Article 99 before we move on to the next highlighted article, which is 121?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we're considering Article 94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said 1994, yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 121 is found on page 19 of the English.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have provision for a constitutional court with the National Assembly electing its presidents and also its members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 135, the next highlighted article, appears at page 21.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This again is another function of the National Assembly, which is to elect judges and public prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Article 140 is found at page 22.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this encompasses the power of the National Assembly to amend the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly, found at tab 97.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these Rules of Procedure were in fact adopted by the Assembly at its session of the 15th of February, but they complement in a fashion the provisions of the constitution that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the first article you've highlighted is Article 26, found at page 3.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This article enumerates the responsibilities of the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course Article 26 continues on to the next page of the English translation. Article 48, the next article, which you've highlighted, is found at page 5.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This article empowers the president of the Assembly to have -- well, what are referred here to as the working bodies, that is, the various commissions of the Assembly, to discuss particular issues and submit a report to the Assembly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe Article 55, found at page -- also found at page 6, addresses committees of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are -- this is a list of the committees or commissions of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 10, Article 82 addresses the power to convene the sessions of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This section of the Rules of Procedure govern the work at sessions, how sessions are to be carried out. And it mentions the right of the president to the Assembly to convene a session on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Articles 89 and 90, found at page 11, appear to address the agenda for the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These articles deal with the responsibility of the presidents of the Assembly in regard to the agenda, that is, the president of the Assembly proposes an agenda at the beginning of the session. Other deputies have a right to add items to that, but the agenda as a whole must then be approved by the entire Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think we can take advantage of the one remaining minute by moving to tab 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think we could deal with it in one minute, Mr. Tieger, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Three articles, Your Honour, Articles 90, 94, and 97, found at page 15, initially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 90 is depicted on the screen in front of you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the article which lists the responsibilities of the government. I think we can skip Article 94, since we've seen it already. It's about the government being responsible to the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Article 97?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 97 addresses the responsibility of the ministries and other administrative agencies to implement the laws enacted by the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no intention of moving on to another document, but perhaps I can assist the Court if there's confusion about the location of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a bit surprised that it seems that we see similar articles starting on page 15, and where we -- it's not entirely clear to me what kind of regulations these are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are articles from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are they any different from what we've seen before from the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the exception of Article 94, which we saw before in relation to the National Assembly, and we didn't dwell on here, these are new articles. They relate to the government rather than the Assembly. These articles are parallel, to a certain extent. They enumerate the powers of the organ under consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question, more precisely, is that what we saw under tab 96, page 15, Article 90, is that any different from what we see on this page 15 under tab 98?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Tabs 90 -- tab 98 was added for convenience, so the Court would not necessarily have to return to 96. I'm sorry it generated confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's part of what we find under 96. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unless I miscalculate, Your Honour, I think we're over our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. And you've dealt with 98?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Treanor, I would like to ask one thing to the parties, but not necessarily in your presence. May I instruct you to -- not to speak with anyone about your testimony, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 o'clock in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what I'd like to ask you is whether we are still on track as far as Mr. Treanor is concerned. As you know, we reserved I think 18 days to start, and then have a -- then have a break of a couple of weeks. I note that we -- you used for the examination of chief, until now, a little bit over 15 hours, almost 15 and a half hours. Mr. Treanor was scheduled for 25 hours. This week we have two days ahead of us. That would -- well, let's say approximately, effectively, eight hours. That would bring us to 23 and a half hours. We lost one day, as you may have noticed, somewhere in the beginning. That also means that if we would have not lost a day, that we would have, without any problem, reached 25 hours. My question to you is: Is it your expectation that we could finish the examination-in-chief of Mr. Treanor by next Friday? If not, perhaps it would be a good idea not to leave one or two hours just hanging for a couple of weeks and see how we could solve that problem. But may I first ask you whether you expect it, in the pace we are moving forwards now, whether you could finish the examination-in-chief of Mr. Treanor by next Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was certainly my intention, Your Honour, and, as you may have noted -- well, I rechecked the number of hours expended at the beginning of this day, and would have answered that question much more confidently at the beginning. It seems that different portions of the material covered move at different paces. It is my -- certainly my intention to do so. I will endeavour to do that, and I'm looking at the material constantly to see if it can be presented to the Court in a more expeditious manner. What I can tell the Court, as I mentioned before, is that we're certainly roughly on schedule, and the period I was focussed on was Friday, as the Court indicated. I also wanted to make every effort to conclude on that date. But some of the material, as the Court may have noted, simply takes more time to address, even when we're moving through it as quickly as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Ms. Loukas, you'd like to respond, or -- because the Chamber has -- perhaps I'll give first an opportunity to you to respond, and it seems that Madam Registrar would also like to have some of my attention. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to indicate that should we fail to complete the evidence on Friday, from the Defence perspective, we're happy to sit on Monday, if that can fit in with the commitments of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, if it were not possible to complete the relevant evidence by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. I'm now waiting for the message. Yes. It's more or less what I expected. The Registrar always helps us out. Of course, if spending the weekend in The Hague unnecessarily, of course, might not be very attractive. There would be a possibility to continue on Friday, also in the afternoon. So we have some additional time on Friday, and this would certainly bring us to the 25 hours, as scheduled. And we'll then have spent 17 1/2 days rather than 18 days. The Chamber would prefer to finish the examination-in-chief of Mr. Treanor before the relatively long pause, since it's not attractive to leave one or two hours of examination in the air for so many weeks. So the parties should prepare that if we have not finished by Friday, a quarter to 2.00, that we might try to find solutions, preferably on Friday, if not possible, then on Monday as well, to finish the examination-in-chief of Mr. Treanor, and perhaps not to start with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in relation to the Friday afternoon option, Your Honour, that's perfectly acceptable, of course, to the Defence. But as for Your Honour's comments about the attractiveness of spending the weekend in The Hague, I must say, the Defence pretty much spends every weekend in The Hague. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of it. I'm doing it already for 25 years. Mr. Tieger, any further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only this, Your Honour: We have attempted to compress these large volumes of material into the projected and predicted time. I would only say this: If we are somewhat over, I think it would represent only a small miscalculation on a very difficult projection to make originally, and we would be asking leave of the Court for permission to extend it somewhat if it was necessary to do so, at least to present the Court with the valuable additional information which might be contained in that portion of the presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that all parties are quite willing to cooperate in such a way that we could finish the examination-in-chief. And let's try to do it within the time limits. If that's completely impossible, let's see how we solve it, but we solve it before the break. We'll then adjourn, with the apologies for the interpreters and the technicians that we took -- we have stolen ten minutes of their time. We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 o'clock, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of February 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
